title: Throwing and Creating Exceptions
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of throwing and creating exceptions in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply throwing and creating exceptions to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Throwing and Creating Exceptions is lesson 109 in Exceptions, Debugging, and Diagnostics. Exceptions represent failures that should interrupt the ordinary path; diagnostics should add actionable context without exposing secrets or hiding the root cause.
content.why_it_matters: Reliable programs expect failure paths and provide information that helps someone diagnose them. This lesson focuses on throwing and creating exceptions and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for throwing and creating exceptions. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: The throw statement
items.text: Catch only failures you can handle, preserve context when rethrowing, and use finally or disposal for cleanup.

items.title: Re-throwing exceptions
items.text: Catch only failures you can handle, preserve context when rethrowing, and use finally or disposal for cleanup.

items.title: Exception constructors
items.text: Make required state explicit during object creation and keep partially initialized objects from escaping.

items.title: Custom exception types
items.text: Catch only failures you can handle, preserve context when rethrowing, and use finally or disposal for cleanup.

items.title: Preserving diagnostic information
items.text: Create a reproducible case, inspect the state at the failure boundary, and log structured context that helps diagnosis.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates throwing and creating exceptions. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates throwing and creating exceptions rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for throwing and creating exceptions before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
